title: Use `peek()` to log/print each employee as the stream pipeline processes them (for debugging only).
shortTitle: Use peek() to log each employee as the stream pipeline processes them (debugging only)
keyPoints: peek(Consumer) runs a side effect on each element then emits the same element unchanged
peek is intermediate and lazy, so a pipeline with no terminal operation runs nothing
Place peek between stages to see how many elements survive each filter or map
A peek before a filter logs all inputs; a peek after it logs only the survivors
The difference between the two logs tells you exactly which records were dropped
peek is a debugging tool: add it temporarily and remove it before production
Since Java 9 a sized stream with a count terminal may skip peek entirely

s1_definition.oneliner: `peek` lets you watch each element go by without changing it: a debugging window into a stream pipeline.
s1_definition.profdef:
peek is the stream equivalent of adding a print statement inside a loop.

- **peek(Consumer)** – takes a consumer, runs it on each element as the element passes that stage, then hands the same element downstream unchanged.
- **Intermediate and lazy** – nothing runs until a terminal operation such as `collect` or `forEach` pulls elements, so `stream().peek(...)` alone does nothing.
- **Diagnostic placement** – put one peek before a filter and one after it to see which records survived and which were dropped.
- **Observation only** – the consumer should not mutate elements or external state; peek is for watching, not working.
- **Temporary** – you add peek while investigating a wrong result and remove it before the code ships.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a conveyor belt of account forms at the National Bank of India. Priya stands beside the belt with a notebook and writes down each form's name as it passes, but she never changes a form; it keeps moving to the next desk. That note-taking is exactly what peek does. If Rajesh wants to know why a report dropped some accounts, he puts Priya before and after the sorting desk and compares her two notebooks.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
PEEK BEFORE AND AFTER A FILTER: FIND THE DROPPED RECORDS

   source           peek IN           filter             peek OUT          count
 ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐   ┌────────┐
 │ staff   │───▶│ log every    │─▶│ salary >     │──▶│ log each    │──▶│ 2      │
 │ stream  │    │ incoming     │  │ 50000        │   │ survivor    │   │        │
 └─────────┘    └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘   └─────────────┘   └────────┘
                      │                   │                 │
                      ▼                   ▼                 ▼
                 IN: Rajesh         drops Priya        OUT: Rajesh
                 IN: Priya          (45000)            OUT: Amit
                 IN: Amit

   Compare logs:  IN has 3 names, OUT has 2  ->  Priya was dropped by the filter


LAZY: NO TERMINAL MEANS NO PEEK

   stream().peek(print)          ──▶  nothing prints (no pull)
   stream().peek(print).count()  ──▶  pulls elements, peek prints (pre Java 9)
   stream().peek(print).count()  ──▶  SIZED, size returned, peek SKIPPED (Java 9+)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When a stream report gives a wrong answer, peek is how you look inside it. It takes a consumer, runs it on each element as the element passes that stage, and hands the same element downstream unchanged. You use it to watch elements move through a pipeline and to see which records survive each filter or map, which is exactly how you diagnose a report at the National Bank of India that returns an unexpected count.

In practice Rajesh places one peek before a filter to log every incoming employee and another peek after the filter to log only the survivors. The difference between the two logs tells him precisely which records were dropped and why. Because peek is lazy, nothing runs until a terminal operation such as collect or count pulls the elements, so a pipeline that ends at peek does nothing, and the log interleaving also reveals that streams push one element all the way through before starting the next.

The point to always add is that peek is strictly for observation. The consumer must not mutate elements or external state, and since Java 9 the pipeline can skip peek entirely when it can compute the result without traversing elements, as a sized stream ending in count does. So peek is never where business logic lives.

Treat peek as a temporary diagnostic that you add while investigating and remove before the code ships. Real transformations go in map, and guaranteed terminal effects go in forEach or a collector. That keeps production code honest and logs clean while still giving you a clear window during debugging.

Remember one sentence: peek is a notebook you hold beside the belt to watch forms go by, not a stamp you use to change them.
